title: The Prophet's pool
hookLine: the Prophet's pool, whiter than milk, where his community drinks
carry: at the prophet's pool, thirst ends for good

lines: A DRY MOUTH, A COLD CUP.
cards: Thirst is about as plain as a feeling gets. A long walk in the heat, a dry mouth, then a cup of cold water, and for a moment nothing else matters.
The hadith collections describe the Day of Judgment as a long, hard standing, and into that picture they place something simple: a pool. Not a palace, not a throne. Water.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, spoke of it to his companions as a place where he would be waiting for them.

teach.h: HAWD: A POOL, A PLACE TO DRINK.
teach.b: The word is hawd, a pool or basin, a place to drink. In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet describes his pool.
Its water is whiter than milk. Its scent is sweeter than musk. Its cups are as many as the stars in the sky.
Its size is a month's journey. And whoever drinks from it will never be thirsty again. Notice what kind of picture this is.
It isn't reward measured in gold. It's thirst ending. Water is the line between life and death, and here that line is drawn for good.
Other reports in Bukhari have him say he will go ahead of his people and be at the pool before them.

His word is farat, and some commentators explain it as the one who rides ahead of a caravan to find water and get the buckets ready. So the picture is personal: someone who went first, waiting at the water with cups.
Some reports also connect the pool to al-Kawthar, the abundance named in Surah al-Kawthar, which opens in Pickthall's translation, "Lo! We have given thee Abundance."

Scholars have discussed how the river and the pool relate, and they don't all describe it the same way. Muslims hold the pool among the unseen things to be believed, without needing to know its shape.
And at an ordinary kitchen sink, the teaching turns a glass of water into a reminder: every time thirst ends, the believer can recall the thirst that ends for good.

how: Muslims affirm the Prophet's pool (al-hawd) as part of belief in the unseen events of the Last Day, drawing on descriptions in the hadith collections; hadith-based manners include saying bismillah before drinking and sipping in a few breaths.

games.q: you've walked all day in the heat, and someone who went ahead of you is standing at the water with a cup. what is the first thing on your mind?
games.why: the hadith's details all serve one point: whoever drinks from it will never be thirsty again.

practice: Take a glass or bottle of water in your hand, or if there's none nearby, simply notice your mouth and your breath. Pause and notice the thirst, small as it is, then take a slow sip and feel it go down.
Muslim table manners, taken from hadith, include saying bismillah first and sipping in a few breaths, so if you pray, say bismillah now; if not, just let the water be water, and let it end a thirst.

wordCard.voice: Hawd. A pool, a basin: the Prophet's pool on the Day, whiter than milk, where his community drinks and is never thirsty again. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a pool or basin where people and animals drink.

carryVoice: Your line: at the prophet's pool, thirst ends for good. Every glass of water can carry a little of it. See you tomorrow.
